vignette:
Dale is a 49-year-old plumber, married, who presented for an initial intake following a referral from his primary care physician. His PCL-5 score of 72 places him in the severe range, and the clinical picture that emerged across the first two sessions is one of a man quietly dismantling his own life in an effort to keep himself safe.

The trauma Dale described occurred in a previous relationship, several years before his current marriage. His former partner, during a period of escalating violence, attacked him in the kitchen of the apartment they shared. He remembers the smell most vividly - something had been left burning on the stove, a sharp, acrid scent that filled the room in the moments before she struck him. The assault was prolonged and humiliating, and Dale has never spoken about it in detail to anyone, including his current wife. What stayed with him was not only the physical pain but the disorientation of being hurt by someone who had also been capable of tenderness, and the particular quality of her voice in the seconds before it happened - low and controlled, not shouting. He had learned, in that relationship, that calm anger was often the most dangerous kind.

Dale works long days as a plumber, moving through residential homes and commercial buildings across the city. It is in this occupational setting that some of his most destabilising moments occur. On a job site several months ago, a homeowner came into the kitchen where Dale was working beneath the sink and began speaking sharply to a family member in the next room - not loudly, but with a clipped, contained irritation. Dale found himself unable to continue working. His hands had gone still, his chest tight, and he had needed to step outside under the pretence of retrieving a tool. More recently, a colleague on a job expressed frustration about a scheduling conflict in a tone that was measured but unmistakably angry. Dale spent the rest of that afternoon watching the man from the corner of his eye, certain, in a way he could not entirely justify to himself, that the situation was about to become dangerous. He had come to believe that other people's anger - even when calm, even when directed elsewhere - was a reliable signal that harm was imminent.

The smell of something burnt is equally destabilising. Dale has walked into kitchens on job sites where something had scorched on the stove, and the sensory familiarity of that smell has, on more than one occasion, produced a sudden and overwhelming sense that he is back in that apartment. Confrontations of any kind - even minor disagreements between other people that he merely witnesses - carry the same charge. These triggers reliably pull him toward a cluster of strategies that, while understandable, have progressively narrowed his life. When a trigger catches him during the day, he finds himself doing whatever is necessary to avoid thinking about the event - redirecting his attention, filling silence with noise, keeping himself occupied until the feeling passes. By evening, the effort of suppression has left him restless and wired, and he has developed a habit of staying up until two or three in the morning, delaying sleep for as long as possible because the quiet of the bedroom is when the images are hardest to push away. The connection is direct and now almost automatic: a trigger encountered during the day creates a pressure that he manages by staying awake at night, cycling through distraction until exhaustion overtakes him.

He has also stopped returning to the neighbourhood where the assault occurred, rerouting his drives and declining job calls in that part of the city, absorbing the professional cost without explanation.

Dale's current wife has noticed that he is tired, short-tempered at times, and increasingly withdrawn in the evenings. She does not know why. What finally brought Dale to seek help was a morning when he arrived at a job, smelled burnt coffee from a break room down the hall, and found that he could not make himself go inside the building. He sat in his truck for forty minutes. He is most afraid, he said quietly, that something is permanently wrong with him - and most hoping, perhaps, that it is not.
